messages.content:
RoadDraft is a headless 2D CAD engine for roadway plans. Model space is US survey feet, and a point is [x, y] = [easting, northing] -- the other way round from how coordinates are usually spoken, so N 5000, E 2000 is [2000, 5000]. Sheets are paper inches seen through viewports at a feet-per-inch scale. Work through the commands: each one validates its params and explains what was wrong, every change is journaled and undoable. Start with get_document_state to see what is in the document, list_commands for the full surface, and render_sheet or render_model to look at your work.

To annotate something, find it before you point at it. In a sheet file the design usually lives in a referenced basefile, so the document owns no geometry of its own; find_entities searches the attachments too. Filter by what a thing IS -- layer, type, or its design anchor -- rather than dumping the document: find_entities {anchor: {kind: 'offset', offset: [-12, 12]}, visible_on: 'C-102'} is the pavement edges that sheet shows. Then pass the id straight to place_callout as target_entity, and the engine puts the leader tip on the geometry. Do not compute the point yourself: the midpoint of a curve's endpoints is not on the curve, and roadway linework runs parallel a few feet apart, so a hand-computed point usually lands on the wrong line rather than on nothing. If you do pass a raw target point, read the warning that comes back -- it names what the tip actually touched.

Some things are not entities at all -- a station, a PC, a point at an offset. Ask the design for those: list_alignments with include_references=true names a referenced alignment 'DESIGN:SR-100', and station_to_xy, xy_to_station, resolve_anchor and get_design_data all accept that name and answer in host coordinates. To call one out, give place_callout a target_anchor ('18+00@12R', 'PC-1'; BC-1 and EC-1 name the PC and PT too) and that alignment name. Otherwise commands do not take it: nothing can be drawn, labelled or anchored to an alignment this document does not own.

Plan annotation belongs on the sheet, in paper inches, not in the model. Pass the sheet as place_callout's space and still name a model target -- target_entity or target_anchor: the engine sees it through the sheet's viewport (scale and twist included) and puts the tip where it shows on the paper. 'at' then runs along the part of the entity that sheet shows, since a pavement edge runs the whole project and a sheet shows one stretch. find_entities with visible_on gives each row a sheet_point, which is where that tip will land -- use it to choose a position for the text that is clear of the linework. Never work out a viewport by hand: model_to_sheet and sheet_to_model convert, and station_to_xy and point_on_entity take a sheet and answer in paper inches as well.

Drafting from a description works the same way: give the engine the description, not coordinates you worked out. A bearing and distance goes in as written -- create_alignment takes start + legs (each leg a bearing, azimuth or deflection and the distance to the next PI, with the radius of the curve at the PI it starts from), draw_traverse draws lines and curves course by course, and traverse computes the points without drawing. offset_entity copies linework parallel at a distance (one entity, or a chain offset as one path), fillet rounds the corner between two lines with a curve (a curb return), and measure with along gives distances along a line, chain or alignment and square off it. key_points and snap give the exact endpoints, intersections, centers and alignment design points (PI, BC, EC) to build on. Station-and-offset drafting is draw_station_offset with the stations and offsets given ('30+00@12R'). Linework drawn through something is cut back with trim (a point on the part to cut away) or run on with extend, not redrawn from computed points; break, join, lengthen, chamfer, copy, rotate, mirror, scale and array edit what is there. create_points sets COGO points, label_segments letters bearings and distances or L1/C1 tags with line and curve tables, place_along sets blocks or points at an interval, hatch fills an area (a point inside is enough), and area and get_entity read areas, lengths, bearings and curve data off the drawing.

Do one drafting task in a headless CAD engine called RoadDraft, using the tools you have been given. They are your ENTIRE tool surface.

Rules:
- Every change to the drawing must go through a tool call.
- The document is already open and saves itself after each command. Do not save it under another name.
- Nobody can answer questions. Work until you judge the task done, then stop and give your report.
- You have no calculator and no code execution. Any arithmetic you need, do yourself.

THE TASK:
Add a right-turn lane to SR-100, on the right side: 12 ft wide, full width from station 31+20 to station 36+00, opened by a 120 ft straight taper that leaves the existing edge of pavement at station 30+00. Draw the new edge of pavement on layer rd_EP -- the taper, the full-width edge, and a square end at 36+00 back to the existing edge.

When finished, reply briefly with:
1. What you created and drew (names, layers, key coordinates).
2. The tool calls that mattered, in order (tool name + the key arguments).
3. Anything that failed, confused you, or that you had to work around -- quote error messages. If you had to compute coordinates yourself, show the arithmetic.

The user wants me to perform a civil engineering drafting task using the provided headless CAD engine tools (RoadDraft).

**Task Breakdown:**
1.  **Goal:** Add a right-turn lane to an existing alignment named `SR-100`.
2.  **Location/Geometry:**
    *   Width: 12 ft wide, on the right side (R).
    *   Stations: From 31+20 to 36+00.
    *   Opening taper: 120 ft straight taper starting at station 30+00.
    *   End condition: Square end at 36+00 back to the existing edge.
3.  **Drawing:** The new edges of pavement (taper, full-width section, square end) must be drawn on layer `rd_EP`.

**Plan:**

1.  **Analyze Existing Geometry:** I need to understand the geometry around the specified stations on `SR-100` to define the start point for the taper and confirm the existing edge line(s). Since the task specifies using "existing edge of pavement at station 30+00," I should use design tools that can handle this.
2.  **Define Taper Start:** The taper starts at 30+00 and lasts 120 ft, connecting to the new full-width section starting at 31+20. Wait, the description says: "opened by a 120 ft straight taper that leaves the existing edge of pavement at station 30+00."
    *   Taper length = 120 ft.
    *   Start Station (S1): 30+00.
    *   End Station (S2): $30+00 + 120/100 = 31+20$. This confirms the geometry aligns with the start of the full-width section.
    *   The taper is drawn *on the right side*. The existing pavement edge at 30+00 defines one end point of the taper, and the new alignment (offset from SR-100) defines the other. I will use `draw_station_offset` or potentially `draw_traverse`/`draw_polyline` if simple lines are sufficient, but since it's related to an offset/pavement edge, `draw_station_offset` seems most appropriate for drawing a segment anchored by stations and offsets.

3.  **Drawing the Components (Using `draw_station_offset`):**
    *   **Taper:** Needs three points: Start Point (Station 30+00), Mid-taper point (for definition, maybe not needed if using station/offset pairs), End Point (Station 31+20). Since it's a straight taper from the existing edge to the new full width offset, I need to define points at:
        *   `BEGIN@Offset_Start`: At Station 30+00. The offset must be 0 or very small, connecting to the existing edge.
        *   Transition point (Mid-taper): This is tricky. `draw_station_offset` connects a chain of points. A straight taper from an existing edge $E_{existing}$ to a new offset $O_{new}$ can be approximated by two offsets: one at the start, and another at the end.
        *   The problem states it *leaves* the existing pavement edge at 30+00. This suggests I need to define the entire profile using station/offset pairs.

    Let's re-read the taper description: "opened by a 120 ft straight taper that leaves the existing edge of pavement at station 30+00."
    *   Station 30+00 (Start): Offset = 0.
    *   Station 31+20 (End): Full width offset is 12 ft (R).

    The geometry is likely a single segment: `[30+00@0]`, followed by points defining the taper, ending at `[31+20@12R]`. However, if I just use these two points, `draw_station_offset` will draw a straight line between them (if `follow=false`). Since it's an *opening*, it should ideally be drawn as a smooth transition/taper. Using only the start and end offsets might be enough for the tool to interpolate a linear taper if I set `follow=False`.

    Let's try defining key points:
    *   Start: `30+00@0` (Station 30+00, Offset 0).
    *   End: `31+20@12R` (Station 31+20, Offset +12 ft Right).

    **Full Width Section:** At station 31+20 to 36+00.
    *   Start: `31+20@12R`.
    *   End: `36+00@12R` (Station 36+00, Offset +12 ft Right).

    **Square End:** At station 36+00 back to the existing edge. This means defining an offset of 0 at 36+00 and running it backward until some point defines the end of the new pavement strip relative to the old one. The prompt says "a square end at 36+00 back to the existing edge." I'll assume this means a short segment defined by station/offset pairs closing off the right side section.

4.  **Executing `draw_station_offset` (Iterative approach):**

    *   **A. Taper:**
        *   Start: 30+00 @ 0 ft offset.
        *   End: 31+20 @ +12 ft R offset.
        *   Points list: `["30+00@0", "31+20@12R"]`. I must set `follow=false` to ensure it treats the transition as a straight taper, not following the alignment curvature unnecessarily if the two offsets are far apart on a curve.

    *   **B. Full Width Section:**
        *   Start: 31+20 @ 12 ft R offset.
        *   End: 36+00 @ 12 ft R offset.
        *   Points list: `["31+20@12R", "36+00@12R"]`. Use `follow=true` (default) or just the two points, as they are parallel offsets along a straight/curved segment.

    *   **C. Square End:**
        *   The pavement ends at 36+00 back to the existing edge. The end point must be defined by its station and offset on the new surface relative to the old one's termination, but the description implies closing off the right side structure. I will define a final segment: Station 36+00 @ 12R (start of cut) to Station X @ 0 (end flush with existing pavement). Since no length is given for the square end, I must assume it starts at the new edge and ends where the original edge was. If I use only two points, it will draw a straight line. Let's assume the "square end" simply means drawing a segment from $36+00@12R$ back to some offset 0 point (maybe slightly past 36+00 for visual closure, but that requires geometry).

    *   **Refining C:** Given the lack of coordinates/stations for the end flush with the old pavement edge, I will draw a segment defined by two points at $36+00$:
        *   Start: `36+00@12R`.
        *   End: I'll assume the square ends when it reaches an offset of 0 from the centerline again (if possible) or simply define a short straight line segment at $36+00$. Since the goal is to *open* the lane, drawing the profile using `draw_station_offset` for all segments seems correct.

    Let's combine them into one sequence of calls, making sure I use the layer `rd_EP`.

**Tool Execution:** (Will start by calling the first segment)
